Question:
Among the cars with an engine displacement of no less than 400 cubic millimeter, how many cars cost at least 30,000?

Evidence:
engine displacement of no less than 400 cubic millimeter refers to displacement > 400; cost at least 30,000 refers to price > 30000
answer: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM data AS T1 INNER JOIN price AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.displacement > 400 AND T2.price > 30000

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the `data` table because it contains each car’s engine displacement, and assign it the target alias: `FROM data AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each car to its price record using the shared `ID` column: `INNER JOIN price AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to cars whose displacement exceeds 400, as specified by the evidence: `WHERE T1.displacement > 400`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the price threshold so that only cars costing more than 30,000 remain: `AND T2.price > 30000`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count all rows that satisfy both conditions by using the aggregate projection: `SELECT COUNT(*)`.

frame styles refers to frameVersion; cards Allen Williams worked on refers to artist = 'Allen Williams'; banned cards refers to status = 'Banned'

prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the frame style, card name, and banned-card indicator, using `DISTINCT` to remove duplicate result rows: `SELECT DISTINCT T1.frameVersion, T1.name, IIF(T2.status = 'Banned', T1.name, 'NO')`.

Question:
For all patients who are older than 55 years old, what is the percentage of female who has abnormal prothrombin time (PT)?

Evidence:
older than 55 years old = SUBTRACT(year(current_timestamp), year(Birthday)) > 55; abnormal prothrombin time (PT) refers to PT > = 14; percentage = DIVIDE(SUM(PT > = 14 AND SEX = 'F'), SUM(PT > = 14)) * 100; female refers to sex = 'F';
answer: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.PT >= 14 AND T1.SEX = 'F' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(*) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.Birthday) > 55

prefix_hints.hint_1: Join each patient’s demographic information to their laboratory records using the shared patient ID: `FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the joined records to patients whose current year minus birth year is greater than 55: `WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.Birthday) > 55`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Identify laboratory rows belonging to female patients with abnormal prothrombin time and count them conditionally: `SUM(CASE WHEN T2.PT >= 14 AND T1.SEX = 'F' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Use the total number of qualifying joined rows as the denominator of the percentage calculation: `COUNT(*)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate the percentage by casting the conditional count to REAL, multiplying by 100, and dividing by the total row count: `SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.PT >= 14 AND T1.SEX = 'F' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(*)`.

Question:
What is the total ordered quantity for products under the 'Touring' line?

Evidence:
The Touring line refers to the product line, therefore ProductLine = 'T'
answer: SELECT SUM(T2.OrderQty) FROM Product AS T1 INNER JOIN PurchaseOrderDetail AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID WHERE T1.ProductLine = 'T'

prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each product to its purchase-order detail records through the shared product identifier: `INNER JOIN PurchaseOrderDetail AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the Touring product line, represented by the code `T`: `WHERE T1.ProductLine = 'T'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Aggregate the ordered quantities from all qualifying purchase-order detail rows: `SUM(T2.OrderQty)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Use the aggregate expression as the query projection, then place it before the product source, join, and Touring filter clauses: `SELECT SUM(T2.OrderQty)`.

Question:
For the goalie who had the most shutouts in 2010, what's his catching hand?

Evidence:
the most shutouts refers to max(SHO); shootCatch = 'L' refers to lefthand; shootCatch = 'R' refers to righthand; shootCatch = 'null' or 'empty' means this player is good at both left and right hand
answer: SELECT T1.shootCatch FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T2.year = 2010 GROUP BY T2.playerID ORDER BY SUM(T2.SHO) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each goalie's biographical record in `Master` to his season statistics in `Goalies` using the shared player identifier: `FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the goalie statistics to the requested 2010 season: `WHERE T2.year = 2010`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Combine multiple stints belonging to the same goalie so that his shutouts can be totaled across all 2010 records: `GROUP BY T2.playerID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank goalies by their summed shutouts from highest to lowest and retain the leader: `ORDER BY SUM(T2.SHO) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the catching-hand value for the top-ranked goalie from the master record; `L` means left, `R` means right, and null or empty indicates both: `SELECT T1.shootCatch`.

Question:
How many flights operated by American Airlines Inc. on 2018/8/1 were faster than scheduled?

Evidence:
American Airlines Inc. refers to Description = 'American Airlines Inc.: AA'; on 2018/8/1 refers to FL_DATE = '2018/8/1'; faster than scheduled refers to ACTUAL_ELAPSED_TIME < CRS_ELAPSED_TIME;
answer: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN T2.ACTUAL_ELAPSED_TIME < CRS_ELAPSED_TIME THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS count FROM Airports AS T1 INNER JOIN Airlines AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.ORIGIN INNER JOIN `Air Carriers` AS T3 ON T2.OP_CARRIER_AIRLINE_ID = T3.Code WHERE T2.FL_DATE = '2018/8/1' AND T3.Description = 'American Airlines Inc.: AA'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Begin with the airport-to-flight relationship used by the target query, matching each flight's origin code to the airport code: `FROM Airports AS T1 INNER JOIN Airlines AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.ORIGIN`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each flight to its operating carrier through the airline identifier and carrier code: `INNER JOIN `Air Carriers` AS T3 ON T2.OP_CARRIER_AIRLINE_ID = T3.Code`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined flight records to the requested date: `WHERE T2.FL_DATE = '2018/8/1'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the carrier-description condition so that only flights operated by American Airlines Inc. remain: `AND T3.Description = 'American Airlines Inc.: AA'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count qualifying flights by conditionally contributing 1 when actual elapsed time is less than scheduled elapsed time, and 0 otherwise: `SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN T2.ACTUAL_ELAPSED_TIME < CRS_ELAPSED_TIME THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS count`.

Question:
How frequently does the first-ever Scheduling Assistant get paid?

Evidence:
PayFrequency = 1 refers to ‘Salary received monthly’; PayFrequency = 2 refers to ‘Salary received biweekly';
answer: SELECT T2.PayFrequency FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.JobTitle = 'Scheduling Assistant' ORDER BY T1.HireDate LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from `Employee`, which contains each employee’s job title and hire date: `FROM Employee AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the employee records to their pay history through the shared business entity identifier: `INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to employees whose job title is Scheduling Assistant: `WHERE T1.JobTitle = 'Scheduling Assistant'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort matching records by hire date so the first-ever hired Scheduling Assistant appears first, then retain that first row: `ORDER BY T1.HireDate LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the pay-frequency code from the matched pay history record; interpret `1` as monthly and `2` as biweekly: `SELECT T2.PayFrequency`.

Question:
Sort in descending order all patients by birthday for male patient with albumin not within range.

Evidence:
male = SEX = 'M'; albumin not within range refers to ALB < = 3.5 or ALB > = 5.5
answer: SELECT DISTINCT T1.ID FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.SEX = 'M' AND (T2.ALB <= 3.5 OR T2.ALB >= 5.5) ORDER BY T1.Birthday DESC

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from patient records and connect each patient to their laboratory results through the shared ID: `FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the joined records to male patients using the SEX value given in the evidence: `WHERE T1.SEX = 'M'`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Add the out-of-range albumin condition, covering values at or below 3.5 and at or above 5.5: `AND (T2.ALB <= 3.5 OR T2.ALB >= 5.5)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Return each qualifying patient ID only once because a patient may have multiple matching laboratory records: `SELECT DISTINCT T1.ID`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Sort the qualifying patients by birthday from latest to earliest with the final ordering clause: `ORDER BY T1.Birthday DESC`.

Question:
List all the pay rates of all employees that were hired at 20 years of age.

Evidence:
pay rate refers to Rate; 20 years old at the time of being hired refers to SUBTRACT(year(HireDate)), (year(BirthDate))) = 20;
answer: SELECT T2.Rate FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', T1.HireDate) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.BirthDate) = 20

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the `Employee` table because it contains both the hire date and birth date needed to determine age at hiring: `FROM Employee AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each employee to their pay history using the shared business entity identifier: `INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.

answer: SELECT T1.cust_name ,  T1.acc_type FROM customer AS T1 JOIN loan AS T2 ON T1.cust_id  =  T2.cust_id GROUP BY T1.cust_name HAVING sum(T2.amount)  >  5000

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the customer table, which provides the customer name and requested account-related field: `FROM customer AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each customer to their loan records through the shared customer identifier: `JOIN loan AS T2 ON T1.cust_id = T2.cust_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined loan records by customer so that each customer’s loan amounts can be aggregated: `GROUP BY T1.cust_name`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only customer groups whose summed loan amount exceeds 5,000: `HAVING sum(T2.amount) > 5000`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the customer name and the account field used by the target query: `SELECT T1.cust_name, T1.acc_type`.

Question:
What is the average quantity of each order for the book "Life Without Fear"?

Evidence:
qty is abbreviation for quantity; average quantity order = AVG(qty)
answer: SELECT CAST(SUM(T2.qty) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.title_id) FROM titles AS T1 INNER JOIN sales AS T2 ON T1.title_id = T2.title_id WHERE T1.title = 'Life Without Fear'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the book catalog and link each title to its sales orders using the shared title identifier: `FROM titles AS T1 INNER JOIN sales AS T2 ON T1.title_id = T2.title_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the joined sales records to the requested book by matching its exact title: `WHERE T1.title = 'Life Without Fear'`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Calculate the total quantity across the matching orders using the sales quantity column: `SUM(T2.qty)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Count the matching order records through their joined title identifiers to obtain the denominator: `COUNT(T1.title_id)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Form the average in the projection by casting the total quantity to REAL before dividing by the order count: `SELECT CAST(SUM(T2.qty) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.title_id)`.

Question:
Among the sales team in South region, write down the numbers of orders made by the sales team ID of one digit.

Evidence:
sales team ID of one digit refers to _SalesTeamID BETWEEN 1 AND 9; numbers of orders refer to COUNT(OrderNumber);
answer: SELECT COUNT(T1.OrderNumber) FROM `Sales Orders` AS T1 INNER JOIN `Sales Team` AS T2 ON T2.SalesTeamID = T1._SalesTeamID WHERE T2.Region = 'South' AND T2.SalesTeamID BETWEEN 1 AND 9 GROUP BY T2.SalesTeamID HAVING COUNT(T1.OrderNumber)

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each sales order to its responsible sales team through the matching team identifier: `FROM `Sales Orders` AS T1 INNER JOIN `Sales Team` AS T2 ON T2.SalesTeamID = T1._SalesTeamID`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the joined records to sales teams assigned to the South region: `WHERE T2.Region = 'South'`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Further restrict the results to one-digit sales team IDs, defined as IDs from 1 through 9: `AND T2.SalesTeamID BETWEEN 1 AND 9`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Create one result group per qualifying sales team and retain groups based on their order count: `GROUP BY T2.SalesTeamID HAVING COUNT(T1.OrderNumber)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the number of orders in each grouped sales team by applying the required aggregate projection: `SELECT COUNT(T1.OrderNumber)`.

Question:
Calculate the difference in the average number of low-priority orders shipped by truck in each month of 1995 and 1996.

Evidence:
SUBTRACT(DIVIDE(SUM(l_orderkey where year(l_shipdate) = 1995), 12), DIVIDE(SUM(l_orderkey where year(l_shipdate) = 1996), 12)) where o_orderpriority = '5-LOW';
answer: SELECT (CAST(SUM(IIF(STRFTIME('%Y', T2.l_shipdate) = 1995, 1, 0)) AS REAL) / 12) - (CAST(SUM(IIF(STRFTIME('%Y', T2.l_shipdate) = 1996, 1, 0)) AS REAL) / 12) FROM orders AS T1 INNER JOIN lineitem AS T2 ON T1.o_orderkey = T2.l_orderkey WHERE T1.o_orderpriority = '5-LOW' AND T2.l_shipmode = 'TRUCK'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each order to its shipped line items using the shared order key so that order priority and shipment details can be analyzed together: `FROM orders AS T1 INNER JOIN lineitem AS T2 ON T1.o_orderkey = T2.l_orderkey`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the joined records to low-priority orders whose line items were shipped by truck: `WHERE T1.o_orderpriority = '5-LOW' AND T2.l_shipmode = 'TRUCK'`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Conditionally count the qualifying shipped line items from 1995 by extracting the year from each ship date: `SUM(IIF(STRFTIME('%Y', T2.l_shipdate) = 1995, 1, 0))`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Build the corresponding conditional count for shipments from 1996: `SUM(IIF(STRFTIME('%Y', T2.l_shipdate) = 1996, 1, 0))`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Convert each annual count to a real-valued monthly average by dividing by 12, then subtract the 1996 average from the 1995 average in the projection: `SELECT (CAST(SUM(IIF(STRFTIME('%Y', T2.l_shipdate) = 1995, 1, 0)) AS REAL) / 12) - (CAST(SUM(IIF(STRFTIME('%Y', T2.l_shipdate) = 1996, 1, 0)) AS REAL) / 12)`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the inventory records to those belonging to store ID 2: `WHERE T2.store_id = 2`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the evidence-based condition that keeps only films with an R rating: `AND T1.rating = 'R'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count the matching film identifiers in the projection to produce the requested total: `SELECT COUNT(T1.film_id)`.

answer: SELECT COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID) FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.Gender = 'M' AND T2.PersonType = 'SP'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the employee records because `Employee` contains both the employee identifier and gender: `FROM Employee AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each employee to the corresponding person record so the `PersonType` classification is available: `INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the employee records to males using the evidence-provided gender code: `WHERE T1.Gender = 'M'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the sales-person classification condition from the `Person` table: `AND T2.PersonType = 'SP'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count the identifiers of employees that satisfy both conditions in the projection: `SELECT COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID)`.

Question:
What is the rental price per day of the most expensive children's film?

Evidence:
children's film refers to name = 'Children'; average price per day of most expensive film = Max(Divide(rental_rate, rental_duration))
answer: SELECT T1.rental_rate FROM film AS T1 INNER JOIN film_category AS T2 ON T1.film_id = T2.film_id INNER JOIN category AS T3 ON T2.category_id = T3.category_id WHERE T3.name = 'Children' ORDER BY T1.rental_rate / T1.rental_duration DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from `film`, which contains both the rental price and rental duration needed to evaluate each film's price per day: `FROM film AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each film to its category assignment through the bridge table using the film identifier: `INNER JOIN film_category AS T2 ON T1.film_id = T2.film_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Join the category records so the category name can be checked for each film: `INNER JOIN category AS T3 ON T2.category_id = T3.category_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only children's films, then rank them from highest to lowest rental price per day: `WHERE T3.name = 'Children' ORDER BY T1.rental_rate / T1.rental_duration DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the rental price of only the top-ranked film by combining the projection and row limit around the preceding clauses: `SELECT T1.rental_rate` and `LIMIT 1`.

Question:

answer: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN T2.year = 2012 THEN T2.grad_cohort ELSE 0 END) - SUM(CASE WHEN T2.year = 2011 THEN T2.grad_cohort ELSE 0 END) FROM institution_details AS T1 INNER JOIN institution_grads AS T2 ON T2.unitid = T1.unitid WHERE T1.chronname = 'Central Alabama Community College'

Question:
Which vendor's selling price for Hex Nut 5 is the lowest, please give the vendor's name.

Evidence:
vendor's selling price refers to StandardPrice; lowest selling price = MIN(StandardPrice)
answer: SELECT T3.Name FROM ProductVendor AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID INNER JOIN Vendor AS T3 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.Name = 'Hex Nut 5' ORDER BY T1.StandardPrice LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from `ProductVendor`, which stores each vendor-product relationship and its selling price in `StandardPrice`: `FROM ProductVendor AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join `Product` so the vendor-product records can be matched to the requested product by its name: `INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Join `Vendor` through the shared business entity identifier to retrieve the vendor's name: `INNER JOIN Vendor AS T3 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the records to the product named Hex Nut 5: `WHERE T2.Name = 'Hex Nut 5'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the vendor name, sort by selling price from lowest to highest, and retain the cheapest result using these clauses: `SELECT T3.Name`, `ORDER BY T1.StandardPrice LIMIT 1`.

answer: SELECT t2.year  ,  SUM ( t2.citation_num ) FROM publication AS t2 JOIN journal AS t1 ON t2.jid  =  t1.jid WHERE t1.name  =  "PVLDB" GROUP BY t2.year;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from publications because each paper’s year, citation count, and journal identifier are stored there: `FROM publication AS t2`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each publication to its journal using the shared journal identifier: `JOIN journal AS t1 ON t2.jid = t1.jid`.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Create one result group for each publication year so citations can be totaled annually: `GROUP BY t2.year`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the year and calculate the sum of citation counts for its group: `SELECT t2.year, SUM(t2.citation_num)`.

Evidence:
restaurant refers to facility_type = 'Restaurant'; on 2015/5/8 refers to inspection_date = '2015-05-08'
answer: SELECT COUNT(T2.license_no) FROM establishment AS T1 INNER JOIN inspection AS T2 ON T1.license_no = T2.license_no WHERE T2.inspection_date = '2015-05-08' AND T1.facility_type = 'Restaurant'

prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each establishment to its inspection records through the shared license number: `INNER JOIN inspection AS T2 ON T1.license_no = T2.license_no`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the inspection records to the specified calendar date: `WHERE T2.inspection_date = '2015-05-08'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Further restrict the matched establishments to restaurants: `AND T1.facility_type = 'Restaurant'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count the license numbers in the qualifying inspection rows to obtain the requested total: `SELECT COUNT(T2.license_no)`.

Question:
When and for what role did the youngest player appear in his first match?

Evidence:
When refers to Match_Date; youngest player refers to max(DOB); first match refers to min(Match_Date)
answer: SELECT T1.Match_Date, T4.Role_Desc FROM `Match` AS T1 INNER JOIN Player_Match AS T2 ON T1.Match_Id = T2.Match_Id INNER JOIN Player AS T3 ON T2.Player_Id = T3.Player_Id INNER JOIN Rolee AS T4 ON T2.Role_Id = T4.Role_Id ORDER BY T3.DOB DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from match records and connect each match to its participating players so the appearance date is available: `FROM `Match` AS T1 INNER JOIN Player_Match AS T2 ON T1.Match_Id = T2.Match_Id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each participation record to the player table, which provides the DOB needed to identify the youngest player: `INNER JOIN Player AS T3 ON T2.Player_Id = T3.Player_Id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Connect the player's match-specific role identifier to its textual description: `INNER JOIN Rolee AS T4 ON T2.Role_Id = T4.Role_Id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Because the youngest player has the latest DOB, sort appearances by DOB from latest to earliest: `ORDER BY T3.DOB DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the match date and role description, then retain the top row after the DOB ordering: `SELECT T1.Match_Date, T4.Role_Desc` and `LIMIT 1`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Count the reporting employees in each manager’s group using the non-null manager reference: `count(T1.reports_to)`.

Question:
What is the stocked quantity of products manufactured from location ID 40?

Evidence:
Stocked quantity refers to StockedQty
answer: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM WorkOrderRouting AS T1 INNER JOIN BillOfMaterials AS T2 ON T1.LocationID = T2.ProductAssemblyID INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS T3 ON T3.WorkOrderID = T1.WorkOrderID WHERE T1.LocationID = 40

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the routing records, which identify the manufacturing location associated with each work order: `FROM WorkOrderRouting AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each routing location to the corresponding product assembly in the bill of materials: `INNER JOIN BillOfMaterials AS T2 ON T1.LocationID = T2.ProductAssemblyID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Link the routing record to its work order by matching their work-order identifiers: `INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS T3 ON T3.WorkOrderID = T1.WorkOrderID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the joined manufacturing records to those associated with location ID 40: `WHERE T1.LocationID = 40`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count all rows that remain after applying the joins and location filter by using this projection at the beginning of the query: `SELECT COUNT(*)`.

Question:
Find the ids of all distinct customers who made order after some orders that were Cancelled.
answer: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM Customer_Orders WHERE order_date  >  (SELECT min(order_date) FROM Customer_Orders WHERE order_status_code  =  "Cancelled")

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use the order records as the source because they contain the customer, status, and date needed for the comparison: `FROM Customer_Orders`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Identify cancelled orders inside a subquery by applying the specified status condition: `WHERE order_status_code = "Cancelled"`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Find the earliest cancelled order date so that any later order occurred after at least one cancelled order: `SELECT min(order_date) FROM Customer_Orders WHERE order_status_code = "Cancelled"`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the outer order records to dates later than the earliest cancelled order date: `WHERE order_date > (SELECT min(order_date) FROM Customer_Orders WHERE order_status_code = "Cancelled")`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return customer identifiers with deduplication because one customer may have multiple qualifying orders: `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id`.

Question:

answer: SELECT T1.Player_Name FROM Player AS T1 INNER JOIN Player_Match AS T2 ON T1.Player_Id = T2.Player_Id INNER JOIN Team AS T3 ON T2.Team_Id = T3.Team_Id INNER JOIN Rolee AS T4 ON T2.Role_Id = T4.Role_Id WHERE T3.Team_Name = 'Rising Pune Supergiants' AND T4.Role_Desc = 'CaptainKeeper' GROUP BY T1.Player_Name

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the player records and connect each player to their match participation, where team and role identifiers are stored: `FROM Player AS T1 INNER JOIN Player_Match AS T2 ON T1.Player_Id = T2.Player_Id`.

Question:
How many matches were held in the league Germany 1. Bundesliga
from August to October 2008?

Evidence:
Germany 1. Bundesliga refers to League.name = 'Germany 1. Bundesliga'; from August to October 2008 refers to strftime('%Y-%m', date) BETWEEN '2008-08' AND '2008-10';
answer: SELECT COUNT(t2.id) FROM League AS t1 INNER JOIN Match AS t2 ON t1.id = t2.league_id WHERE t1.name = 'Germany 1. Bundesliga' AND SUBSTR(t2.`date`, 1, 7) BETWEEN '2008-08' AND '2008-10'

prefix_hints.hint_2: Add instructors by joining them to the same department, allowing both populations to be counted per department: `JOIN instructor AS T3 ON T1.dept_name = T3.dept_name`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Create one aggregate group for each department represented by the instructor records: `GROUP BY T3.dept_name`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Count distinct student IDs because joining students and instructors can create multiple rows for the same student: `count(DISTINCT T2.id)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the distinct student count, distinct instructor count, and department name in the requested output: `SELECT count(DISTINCT T2.id), count(DISTINCT T3.id), T3.dept_name`.

Question:
What is the highest lake area coverage of a country?

Evidence:
Lake area coverage = [sum(area of the lakes in the country) / (area of the country)] * 100%
answer: SELECT T2.Area * 100  / T3.Area FROM located AS T1 INNER JOIN lake AS T2 ON T1.Lake = T2.Name INNER JOIN country AS T3 ON T3.Code = T1.Country ORDER BY T2.Longitude DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_3: Join the country record using its code to obtain the country's total area: `INNER JOIN country AS T3 ON T3.Code = T1.Country`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Calculate the percentage coverage by multiplying the lake area by 100 and dividing by the country area: `SELECT T2.Area * 100 / T3.Area`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Sort the candidate rows by lake longitude in descending order and retain the first result: `ORDER BY T2.Longitude DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:

Evidence:
home manufactured refers to MakeFlag = 1; average rating = divide(sum(Rating), count(ProductReview))
answer: SELECT T2.Name FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID WHERE T2.MakeFlag = 1 GROUP BY T2.Name ORDER BY SUM(T1.Rating) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Connect each review to its product so the product name and manufacturing flag are available alongside the rating: `FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Create one result group for each product name so its review ratings can be aggregated: `GROUP BY T2.Name`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the grouped products by the sum of their ratings in descending order, as specified by the target query: `ORDER BY SUM(T1.Rating) DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the product name and retain only the highest-ranked result by placing `SELECT T2.Name` at the beginning and `LIMIT 1` after the ordering clause.

Question:
Find the id of the order which is shipped most recently.
answer: SELECT order_id FROM shipments WHERE shipment_date  =  (SELECT max(shipment_date) FROM shipments)

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use the `shipments` table because it contains both the order identifier and shipment date: `FROM shipments`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Determine the latest shipment date by applying the maximum aggregate to the shipment date column: `max(shipment_date)`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Turn that aggregate into a scalar subquery that returns the most recent date across all shipments: `(SELECT max(shipment_date) FROM shipments)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep shipments whose date equals the latest date returned by the subquery: `WHERE shipment_date = (SELECT max(shipment_date) FROM shipments)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the order identifier from each qualifying shipment by placing this clause before the source and filter clauses: `SELECT order_id`.

answer: SELECT T2.Player FROM country AS T1 JOIN match_season AS T2 ON T1.Country_id  =  T2.Country WHERE T1.Country_name  =  "Indonesia"

prefix_hints.hint_3: Apply the evidence definition of “no fine” by retaining violations whose fine equals zero: `WHERE T2.fine = 0`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Use the point-level column from the inspection-point table as the result expression: `T1.point_level`.

Question:
Which religion is most prevalent in Asia?

Evidence:
Most prevalent religion refers to the religion with the most population percentage
answer: SELECT T4.Name FROM continent AS T1 INNER JOIN encompasses AS T2 ON T1.Name = T2.Continent INNER JOIN country AS T3 ON T3.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN religion AS T4 ON T4.Country = T3.Code WHERE T1.Name = 'Asia' GROUP BY T4.Name ORDER BY SUM(T4.Percentage) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from continents and connect each continent to its associated countries through `encompasses`: `FROM continent AS T1 INNER JOIN encompasses AS T2 ON T1.Name = T2.Continent`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link the encompassed country codes to the corresponding country records, then connect those countries to their religions: `INNER JOIN country AS T3 ON T3.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN religion AS T4 ON T4.Country = T3.Code`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to countries associated with Asia: `WHERE T1.Name = 'Asia'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Combine records by religion name and rank religions by the descending sum of their population percentages: `GROUP BY T4.Name ORDER BY SUM(T4.Percentage) DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the name of the highest-ranked religion by using the projection and one-row limit: `SELECT T4.Name` and `LIMIT 1`.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Compute the number of service records within each service-type group using the aggregate expression: `COUNT(*)`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Rank the joined records from the highest to the lowest high estimate: `ORDER BY high_estimate DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only the first record after sorting so that the result corresponds to the maximum high estimate: `LIMIT 1`.

Question:
What is given name for player 'aebisda01'. Calculate the average time in minutes for the all his games played as goaltender.

Evidence:
played as goaltender refers to pos = 'G'; time in minutes refers to Min; all his games played refers to GP; average time in minutes refers to DIVIDE(SUM(Min)/SUM(GP))
answer: SELECT T1.nameGiven, CAST(SUM(T2.Min) AS REAL) / SUM(T2.GP) FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T1.playerID = 'aebisda01' GROUP BY T1.nameGiven

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the player profile table, where the given name and player identifier are stored: `FROM Master AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link the player profile to all of his goaltender records using the shared player identifier: `INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the requested player: `WHERE T1.playerID = 'aebisda01'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Group the records by the player's given name so the goaltender totals can be aggregated across all seasons and stints: `GROUP BY T1.nameGiven`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the given name and calculate minutes per game by dividing total minutes by total games played, casting the numerator to REAL for decimal division: `SELECT T1.nameGiven, CAST(SUM(T2.Min) AS REAL) / SUM(T2.GP)`.

prefix_hints.hint_1: Build the inner query’s customer-policy relationship so each policy can be counted for its customer: `FROM customers AS t1 JOIN customers_policies AS t2 ON t1.customer_id = t2.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Group those policy records by customer name, then rank customers by policy count and retain the top one: `GROUP BY t1.customer_name ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Project the top customer’s name from the inner query so it can be used as the outer filter value: `SELECT t1.customer_name`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: In the outer query, connect customers to their policies and then to the policy details containing the type codes: `FROM customers AS t1 JOIN customers_policies AS t2 ON t1.customer_id = t2.customer_id JOIN available_policies AS t3 ON t2.policy_id = t3.policy_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Filter the outer rows to the customer returned by the top-customer subquery, and project each policy type only once using `WHERE t1.customer_name = (SELECT t1.customer_name FROM customers AS t1 JOIN customers_policies AS t2 ON t1.customer_id = t2.customer_id GROUP BY t1.customer_name ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1)` together with `SELECT DISTINCT t3.policy_type_code`.

Question:
Find all the forenames of distinct drivers who was in position 1 as standing and won?
answer: SELECT DISTINCT T1.forename FROM drivers AS T1 JOIN driverstandings AS T2 ON T1.driverid = T2.driverid WHERE T2.position = 1 AND T2.wins = 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the `drivers` table because it contains each driver's forename: `FROM drivers AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the standings records to each driver through their shared driver identifier: `JOIN driverstandings AS T2 ON T1.driverid = T2.driverid`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to standings where the driver was in first position: `WHERE T2.position = 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the requirement that the first-position standings record also reports one win: `AND T2.wins = 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the drivers' forenames and remove duplicates caused by multiple qualifying standings records: `SELECT DISTINCT T1.forename`.

Question:
What is the total salary expenses of team Boston Red Stockings in 2010?
answer: SELECT sum(T1.salary) FROM salary AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  = 'Boston Red Stockings' AND T1.year  =  2010

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the salary records because they contain the individual salary amounts to be totaled: `FROM salary AS T1`.

Question:
For the user who gave the most number of long reviews, what is his/her averge ratings of all review?

Evidence:
long reviews refers to review_length = 'long'; most number of long reviews refers to MAX(COUNT(review_length = 'long')); average ratings = AVG(review_stars);
answer: SELECT CAST(SUM(T1.review_stars) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.review_stars) FROM Reviews AS T1 INNER JOIN Users AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id WHERE T1.review_length LIKE 'Long' GROUP BY T1.user_id ORDER BY COUNT(T1.review_length) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each review to its author through the shared user identifier: `FROM Reviews AS T1 INNER JOIN Users AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the records to reviews classified as long using the review-length label: `WHERE T1.review_length LIKE 'Long'`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the filtered reviews by author so each user's long-review count and ratings can be evaluated separately: `GROUP BY T1.user_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank users by their number of long reviews and retain only the user with the highest count: `ORDER BY COUNT(T1.review_length) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate that selected user's average review rating by dividing the real-valued sum of review stars by their count: `SELECT CAST(SUM(T1.review_stars) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.review_stars)`.

Question:
On what year did the youngest driver had his first qualifying race? Also state the name, date and time of the race.

answer: SELECT T3.year, T3.name, T3.date, T3.time FROM qualifying AS T1 INNER JOIN drivers AS T2 on T1.driverId = T2.driverId INNER JOIN races AS T3 on T1.raceId = T3.raceId WHERE T1.driverId = ( SELECT driverId FROM drivers ORDER BY dob DESC LIMIT 1 ) ORDER BY T3.date ASC LIMIT 1

answer: SELECT (SUM(CASE WHEN t1.player_name = 'Landon Donovan' THEN t2.overall_rating ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 - SUM(CASE WHEN t1.player_name = 'Jordan Bowery' THEN t2.overall_rating ELSE 0 END)) * 100 / SUM(CASE WHEN t1.player_name = 'Landon Donovan' THEN t2.overall_rating ELSE 0 END) LvsJ_percent FROM Player AS t1 INNER JOIN Player_Attributes AS t2 ON t1.player_fifa_api_id = t2.player_fifa_api_id WHERE SUBSTR(t2.`date`, 1, 10) = '2013-07-12'

answer: SELECT T2.roomName FROM Reservations AS T1 JOIN Rooms AS T2 ON T1.Room  =  T2.RoomId GROUP BY T1.Room ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the reservation records, since each row represents one reservation: `FROM Reservations AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each reservation to its room record so the corresponding room name is available: `JOIN Rooms AS T2 ON T1.Room = T2.RoomId`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined reservation rows by room so that reservations can be counted separately for each room: `GROUP BY T1.Room`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the room groups from the greatest reservation count to the smallest and retain only the top group: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the name of the highest-ranked room from the joined `Rooms` table: `SELECT T2.roomName`.

What is the full name of the employee who has the most customers?

Question:
Show the most common apartment type code among apartments with more than 1 bathroom.
answer: SELECT apt_type_code FROM Apartments WHERE bathroom_count  >  1 GROUP BY apt_type_code ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use the `Apartments` table because it contains both the apartment type and bathroom count: `FROM Apartments`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the rows to apartments having more than one bathroom: `WHERE bathroom_count > 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the qualifying apartments by type so the number of apartments in each type can be counted: `GROUP BY apt_type_code`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the apartment-type groups from most common to least common using their row counts: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the apartment type code and keep only the highest-ranked group by combining the projection `SELECT apt_type_code` with the final restriction `LIMIT 1`.

B refers to grade; GPA is an abbreviated name of Grade Point Average where over 3 refers to gpa > 3;

prefix_hints.hint_3: Use the `registration` table as the outer source and restrict registrations to grade B: `FROM registration WHERE grade = 'B'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Further restrict those B-grade registrations to student identifiers returned by the GPA-and-course subquery: `AND student_id IN ( SELECT student_id FROM student WHERE gpa > 3 AND course_id IN ( SELECT course_id FROM course WHERE name = 'Machine Learning Theory' ) )`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count the qualifying student identifiers by placing this aggregate in the outer projection: `SELECT COUNT(student_id)`.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only the first ranked course, which is the one with the most registered students: `LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the name of the highest-ranked course through the projection clause: `SELECT T1.course_name`.

Question:
Calculate the average length of employment for employee working in the Research and Development deparment.

Evidence:
average length of employment = AVG(subtract(2022, year(HireDate)))
answer: SELECT AVG(STRFTIME('%Y', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.HireDate)) FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Department AS T3 ON T2.DepartmentID = T3.DepartmentID WHERE T3.Name = 'Research and Development'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from employee records because `HireDate` is stored in `Employee`, then connect each employee to their department history using the shared business entity identifier: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the department history to `Department` so that the department name is available for filtering: `INNER JOIN Department AS T3 ON T2.DepartmentID = T3.DepartmentID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to employees associated with the Research and Development department: `WHERE T3.Name = 'Research and Development'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Calculate each employee's employment length in years by subtracting the hire year from the current year with SQLite's `STRFTIME` function: `STRFTIME('%Y', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.HireDate)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Average the calculated employment lengths by placing the year-difference expression inside `AVG` in the projection: `SELECT AVG(STRFTIME('%Y', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.HireDate))`.

Question:
What is the difference in salary of the top 2 employees with the highest number of territories in charge?

Evidence:
highest number of territories refers to max(TerritoryID); difference in salary = subtract(employeeA.Salary, employeeB.Salary)
answer: SELECT MAX(Salary) - MIN(Salary) FROM ( SELECT T1.Salary FROM Employees AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeTerritories AS T2 ON T1.EmployeeID = T2.EmployeeID GROUP BY T1.EmployeeID, T1.Salary ORDER BY COUNT(T2.TerritoryID) DESC LIMIT 2 ) T1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each employee to their assigned territories using the shared employee identifier: `FROM Employees AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeTerritories AS T2 ON T1.EmployeeID = T2.EmployeeID`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Group the joined rows by employee so each employee’s territory assignments can be counted while retaining the salary: `GROUP BY T1.EmployeeID, T1.Salary`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Rank employees from the greatest number of assigned territories to the least: `ORDER BY COUNT(T2.TerritoryID) DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Project the salary from this ranking and retain only the two highest-ranked employees, then use the result as a derived table: `SELECT T1.Salary ... LIMIT 2 ) T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate the salary difference between those two employees by subtracting the smaller salary from the larger one in the outer projection: `SELECT MAX(Salary) - MIN(Salary) FROM ( ... ) T1`.

Question:
How many Haileybury Hockey Club goalies became a hall of famer?

Evidence:
hall of famers refers to hofID where playerID is not NULL;
answer: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.playerID) FROM Goalies AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID INNER JOIN Teams AS T3 ON T1.tmID = T3.tmID AND T1.year = T3.year WHERE T3.name = 'Haileybury Hockey Club' AND T2.hofID IS NOT NULL

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from goalie records and connect each goalie to the corresponding person in `Master` through `playerID`: `FROM Goalies AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each goalie season to the correct team using both the team identifier and year, since a team ID can occur across multiple seasons: `INNER JOIN Teams AS T3 ON T1.tmID = T3.tmID AND T1.year = T3.year`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to goalies who played for the named club: `WHERE T3.name = 'Haileybury Hockey Club'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Apply the evidence-based Hall of Fame condition by retaining players whose `hofID` is populated: `AND T2.hofID IS NOT NULL`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count unique qualifying goalies so a player appearing in multiple seasons or stints is counted once: `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.playerID)`.

Question:
Find the top 3 products which have the largest number of problems?
answer: SELECT T2.product_name FROM problems AS T1 JOIN product AS T2 ON T1.product_id = T2.product_id GROUP BY T2.product_name ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the problem records, since each row represents a problem associated with a product: `FROM problems AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each problem to its product so the corresponding product name is available: `JOIN product AS T2 ON T1.product_id = T2.product_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined problem rows by product name so `count(*)` measures the number of problems for each product: `GROUP BY T2.product_name`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank products from the largest problem count to the smallest and retain only the first three: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the names of the three qualifying products by placing this clause before the joined, grouped, and ranked data: `SELECT T2.product_name`.

total purchase price including freight refers to add(multiply(UnitPrice , Quantity) , Freight); most expensive refers to max(UnitPrice)
answer: SELECT T2.UnitPrice * T2.Quantity + T1.Freight FROM Orders AS T1 INNER JOIN `Order Details` AS T2 ON T1.OrderID = T2.OrderID ORDER BY T2.UnitPrice * T2.Quantity + T1.Freight DESC LIMIT 2

prefix_hints.hint_3: Calculate the purchase price including freight by multiplying unit price by quantity and then adding freight: `T2.UnitPrice * T2.Quantity + T1.Freight`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the calculated purchase prices from highest to lowest to put the most expensive entries first: `ORDER BY T2.UnitPrice * T2.Quantity + T1.Freight DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the calculated total and retain only the first two ranked entries using these clauses: `SELECT T2.UnitPrice * T2.Quantity + T1.Freight` and `LIMIT 2`.

Question:
What is the product with the most profit?

Evidence:
profit = SUBTRACT(ListPrice, StandardCost);
answer: SELECT T1.ProductID FROM ProductListPriceHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductCostHistory AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID ORDER BY T1.ListPrice - T2.StandardCost DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Begin with the price-history table because it contains each product's historical `ListPrice`: `FROM ProductListPriceHistory AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the corresponding cost-history records through the shared product identifier so each price can be compared with a standard cost: `INNER JOIN ProductCostHistory AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Calculate profit by subtracting the standard cost from the list price, following the provided definition: `T1.ListPrice - T2.StandardCost`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the joined records from greatest profit to least profit: `ORDER BY T1.ListPrice - T2.StandardCost DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the product identifier and retain only the first record in the profit ranking: `SELECT T1.ProductID` and `LIMIT 1`.

Question:
What is the name of the university with the most international students in 2011?

Evidence:
in 2011 refers to year 2011; the most international students refers to MAX(DIVIDE(MULTIPLY(num_students,  pct_international_students), 100)); name of university refers to university_id
answer: SELECT T2.university_name FROM university_year AS T1 INNER JOIN university AS T2 ON T1.university_id = T2.id WHERE T1.year = 2011 ORDER BY T1.pct_international_students DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the yearly university statistics, which contain the year and international-student percentage: `FROM university_year AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each yearly record to its university so its name can be retrieved: `INNER JOIN university AS T2 ON T1.university_id = T2.id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the statistics to the requested year: `WHERE T1.year = 2011`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the universities from highest to lowest international-student percentage: `ORDER BY T1.pct_international_students DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the university name and keep only the top-ranked row by using the projection `SELECT T2.university_name` together with `LIMIT 1`.

Question:
List the store ID of the films with a rental rate greater than the 60% of average rental rate of all listed films.

Evidence:
average rental rate of all listed films refers to AVG(rental_rate); rental rate greater than the 60% of average rental rate refers to rental_rate > (AVG(rental_rate)) MULTIPLY 0.6
answer: SELECT T2.store_id FROM film AS T1 INNER JOIN inventory AS T2 ON T1.film_id = T2.film_id WHERE T1.rental_rate > ( SELECT AVG(T1.rental_rate) * 0.6 FROM film AS T1 )

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the `film` table, which contains each film’s rental rate and film identifier: `FROM film AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each film to its inventory records so the associated store ID becomes available: `INNER JOIN inventory AS T2 ON T1.film_id = T2.film_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Calculate the average rental rate across all listed films in a scalar subquery: `SELECT AVG(T1.rental_rate) FROM film AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Multiply that average by 0.6 and retain films whose rental rate exceeds the resulting threshold: `WHERE T1.rental_rate > ( SELECT AVG(T1.rental_rate) * 0.6 FROM film AS T1 )`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the store identifier from the matched inventory records in the outer query: `SELECT T2.store_id`.

Question:
For the employee who has been hired the latest, what is his or her pay rate?

Evidence:
hired the latest refers to max(HireDate)
answer: SELECT T1.Rate FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID ORDER BY T2.HireDate DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the pay history table because the requested pay rate is stored in its `Rate` column: `FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each pay-history record to its employee using the shared business entity identifier: `INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Place the most recently hired employee first by sorting the employee hire date in descending order: `ORDER BY T2.HireDate DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only the first row after sorting so the result corresponds to the latest hire: `LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the pay rate from the pay-history table by placing this clause at the beginning of the assembled query: `SELECT T1.Rate`.

prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the locations to Mountain View by filtering on the location table’s city name: `WHERE t2.city_name = "mountain view"`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Narrow the results to restaurants serving Arabic food: `AND t1.food_type = "arabic"`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Interpret a good restaurant as one with a rating above 2.5 and add that quality condition: `AND t1.rating > 2.5`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the restaurant’s house number and name by placing this projection before the join and filters: `SELECT t2.house_number, t1.name`.

What is the film title and inventory id of the item in the inventory which was rented most frequently?
answer: SELECT T1.title ,  T2.inventory_id FROM film AS T1 JOIN inventory AS T2 ON T1.film_id  =  T2.film_id JOIN rental AS T3 ON T2.inventory_id  =  T3.inventory_id GROUP BY T2.inventory_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each inventory copy to its rental records so that every row represents one rental occurrence for that item: `JOIN rental AS T3 ON T2.inventory_id = T3.inventory_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Aggregate the rental rows separately for each physical inventory item: `GROUP BY T2.inventory_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank inventory items by rental frequency from highest to lowest and retain only the most frequently rented one: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the film title and inventory identifier for the top-ranked item at the beginning of the assembled query: `SELECT T1.title, T2.inventory_id`.
